title: I feel like this review makes it sound like I hate the original play ...
transcript: Between the stacked line up of Broadway stars, the Pulitzer-winning source material, and a writer I love, this new musical has been one of my most anticipated shows of the season. The end result was pretty much the definition of a mixed bag for me, but there's a lot about it that I loved. So for the nerds out there, here are my deep dive thoughts on the Seat of Our Pants a new musical by Ethan Lipton based on the Thornton Wilder play The Skin of Our Teeth, which some of you might remember from the admittedly superior Broadway revival from a couple years ago. Or you might remember from my sophomore year high school production, where I was catastrophically miscast as Mr. Antrobus because there weren't enough boys. But I digress. So for those who don't know the play, it's a pretty kooky, time-bending allegory for the human race surviving in the face of catastrophe. It's absurd, it breaks the fourth wall, and it's a lot of things at once. First thing I'll say is that the score is kinda simple and folksy and I really enjoyed it. I thought it brought a grounded humanity that doesn't come naturally to this play. A great example is this lyric at the end of Act 1, when the ice wall is approaching and they sing, “we were born out of the darkness.” “If the darkness calls us back,” “let us pray smell a brisket, as we step into the black.” These unexpected references to quotidian details of human life were sprinkled throughout the score, and I kinda loved it. Even though the original play ostensibly deals with the universal human experience, it can also feel a bit too heady and allegorical. And I think Ethan Lipton's best contributions were the ones that helped us connect back to that grounded, relatable humanity. In the case of that example, not just the acute fear of death, but the little things, like the smell of brisket, that form the simple but powerful joys of living. And I also find it really funny in that distinctly Ethan Lipton way that allows silliness and earnestness to feel in harmony with each other, if not one and the same. I did have mixed feelings about the placement of the songs, though. Sometimes it was pretty standard or traditional, sometimes it was deliberately abrupt in a good way, and sometimes not. There's one song that's literally just one line long, and it's just like, what? What was that? But I kind of thought it was hilarious. But then other songs felt shoehorned in a way that really didn't work for me at all. I had the feeling that I often have with musicals based on popular plays, which is that I wish more of it was musicalized to help solidify its own sense of identity and not just feel like the play with songs added. In the Program notes Ethan Lipton talks about learning to be less deferential and more authorial in the adaptation process, but watching this adaptation, I actually thought he could would have gone a lot further with that. There are plenty of moments where he injects his own sensibilities, but I wonder what it would have looked like if he had retained almost none of the original dialogue and just filtered the whole story through his own voice from the ground up. This version of the show feels almost like a conversation between Wilder and Lipton, which I think was the point. And it is interesting in its own way. I mentioned earlier how that worked well for me with the lyrics, but when it came to the more overt references to Modern Day, to Thornton Wilder, to the original play, it's not that it didn't work or make sense, as much as I don't think we got anywhere sufficiently new or interesting with it that the original play didn't already say for itself. The direction and performances also felt a bit hit or miss to me, the highlight definitely being Michaela Diamond as Sabina. Fantastic performance, but a lot of the other actors felt a little lost to me. Despite all my criticisms, though, I think I still landed slightly more positive than negative, which might have to do with the goodwill I already had toward the play and Ethan Lipton's past work in general. I think he and I are on the same wavelength in a lot of ways. So even when it didn't totally work for me, I was pretty thoroughly fascinated by it. And considering the source material we're working with here, there's something fitting, almost even endearing, about a messy and inconsistent adaptation.
